title: When and Where to Reset Matters for Long-Term Test-Time Adaptation
claim: Reset only when accumulated error signals collapse risk, and only the affected parts, rather than resetting everything on a fixed schedule.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right; input streams feed a layer stack and reset-decision boxes
description: The figure reads left to right. At the far left, a 'Long Domain Stream' of colored bars is unpacked into an 'Online Batch Stream' of batches, each a dashed box of green squares. Three columns follow, each a four-layer network stack with an input batch of numbered shapes below and a predicted-output batch above. Layer shading goes from pale pink to deep red across the columns, showing accumulated error. Above each column is a small bar chart comparing current concentration C_t with cumulative concentration C̄_{t-1}. Predictions drift toward one repeated class, as in the '3 3 3' with dark shapes. Green arrows lead to two rounded boxes, 'Adaptive Reset by C_t > C̄_{t-1}' and 'Selective Reset with C_t − C̄_{t-1} (Eq. 3)'. The result is a rightmost stack in which most layers are reset to white and one stays pink. Predictions there are diverse again, '1 3 4'. A small legend defines the C terms.
caption: Illustrative comparison between a naive reset approach (RDumb; [ref]) and our Adaptive and Selective Reset (ASR) based on the same model (ETA; [ref]). RDumb fully resets parameters at fixed intervals (e.g., every 1000 steps), whereas ASR dynamically decides when and where to reset, achieving more stable (i.e., less abrupt performance drop at each reset) and higher performance. Dotted vertical lines indicate when resets occur.
abstract: When continual test-time adaptation (TTA) persists over the long term, errors accumulate in the model and further cause it to predict only a few classes for all inputs, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Recent studies have explored reset strategies that completely erase these accumulated errors. However, their periodic resets lead to suboptimal adaptation, as they occur independently of the actual risk of collapse. Moreover, their full resets cause catastrophic loss of knowledge acquired over time, even though such knowledge could be beneficial in the future. To this end, we propose (1) an Adaptive and Selective Reset (ASR) scheme that dynamically determines when and where to reset, (2) an importance-aware regularizer to recover essential knowledge lost due to reset, and (3) an on-the-fly adaptation adjustment scheme to enhance adaptability under challenging domain shifts. Extensive experiments across long-term TTA benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly under challenging conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/YonseiML/asr.
